lesson.title: Straight, Curved, or Scattered: The Form of an Association
lesson.summary: Learn to distinguish linear from nonlinear, curved, patterns in a scatterplot, and understand why identifying form correctly must happen before trusting any single summary statistic.
lesson.body:
After you have described whether an association trends positively or negatively, the next question a statistician asks is about its form: what shape does the pattern in the scatterplot actually take? Direction only tells you whether the cloud of points goes up or down, form tells you whether that up-or-down trend follows a straight line, bends into a curve, or shows no describable pattern whatsoever.

Form generally falls into a few broad categories. A linear form means the points cluster around what looks like a straight line, rising or falling at a roughly constant rate across the whole range of the data. A nonlinear, or curved, form means the points bend, perhaps rising quickly at first and then leveling off, or curving upward like a parabola, so that a single straight line would badly misrepresent parts of the pattern. And some scatterplots show no discernible form at all, just a formless cloud of points with no consistent shape, which usually signals little or no association between the two variables.

The study hours and exam score data from earlier, (1, 68) through (6, 90), has a form that is close to linear: the points rise at a fairly steady rate, with the exam score gaining roughly four or five points for each additional hour studied. Contrast that with something like the relationship between a car's speed and its braking distance, where the pattern bends upward, growing faster and faster as speed increases rather than climbing at a constant rate. That second example has a nonlinear form, and you will look at it in detail in the next chapter.

Identifying form correctly matters because it decides which tools you are allowed to use later. The correlation coefficient, which you will meet soon, is built specifically to measure the strength of a linear form, it can be badly misleading when applied to a relationship that is actually curved. A strong, perfectly predictable curved pattern can produce a correlation coefficient close to zero, falsely suggesting no relationship exists, simply because r has no way to detect a bend. This is why examining form always comes before trusting a single summary number: the shape of the scatterplot decides which numerical summaries are even appropriate to compute.

In practice, checking form is mostly a visual skill at this stage of the course: look at the scatterplot and ask whether a single straight line, drawn by eye through the middle of the cloud, would follow the points reasonably well across their entire range, from the smallest explanatory value to the largest. If the line fits the left side of the data but drifts away from the points on the right side, or vice versa, the form is not linear no matter how tight the overall pattern looks.

This habit of checking for a straight-line pattern before trusting further calculations should feel familiar. It is the same instinct you practiced with the normal probability plot, where a straight line indicated approximate normality and curvature signaled a departure from it. In both cases, the shape of the plot, not just a single computed number, is where the real diagnostic information lives.
